TRIN-B1C0: This introductory note reproduces Augustine's Retractations account and his cover letter to Bishop Aurelius explaining that the work was stolen and circulated in an unfinished, uncorrected state, forcing him to complete and publish it as best he could.
TRIN-B1C1: Augustine explains he writes against three classes of people who err about God: those who picture Him in bodily terms, those who project the soul's own changeable nature onto Him, and the presumptuous who overreach reason, arguing that Scripture nourishes weak minds with condescending, bodily and creaturely language so as to lead them by degrees toward the truly ineffable and unchangeable.
TRIN-B1C2: Augustine states his plan: with God's help he will show from Scripture that the Trinity is the one true God of one substance, hoping even quarrelsome disputants may find something they cannot doubt and so be drawn back from proud argument to the healing discipline of faith.
TRIN-B1C3: Augustine asks his readers to advance with him wherever they agree, inquire together wherever they doubt, and correct him wherever he errs, insisting that a reader's failure to understand his language is a fault of style, not of the faith he professes, and that varied treatments by many authors serve different readers.
TRIN-B1C4: Augustine sets out the Catholic rule of faith he intends to defend: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God of one substance in indivisible equality, three distinct persons, yet it is only the Son who was born of the Virgin and crucified and only the Spirit who appeared as a dove, even though the Trinity as a whole works indivisibly.
TRIN-B1C5: Augustine names the standing puzzle inquirers raise: if the three Persons work indivisibly in everything, how could the Father's voice at the Jordan, the Son's incarnate birth, and the Spirit's appearance as a dove each belong to only one Person, and how can the Spirit, begotten by neither, still be the Spirit of both Father and Son.
TRIN-B1C6: Marshaling John 1:1-3 and 1 Timothy 6:15-16, Augustine argues the Son is true God of one substance with the Father because 'all things were made by Him' and He is therefore not a creature, and that the Holy Spirit likewise is not a creature but true God, since Scripture commands the exclusive worship (latria) owed to God alone to be rendered to the Spirit as the temple of whom our bodies are called.
TRIN-B1C7: Augustine introduces the interpretive rule that will govern the rest of the work: texts calling the Son less than the Father, such as 'My Father is greater than I,' refer to the 'form of a servant' the Word took on in the Incarnation, while texts affirming His equality refer to the eternal 'form of God,' so that the same Son is, in a sense, even less than His own unincarnate self.
TRIN-B1C8: Applying the form-of-God/form-of-servant rule to 1 Corinthians 15's 'then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him,' Augustine argues that Christ's 'delivering up the kingdom' to the Father means bringing the redeemed from believing by faith to beholding God face to face, not that His human nature will be transformed into the divine substance or that He will cease to reign.
TRIN-B1C9: Augustine shows that because the three Persons are inseparable, Scripture's naming of one Person alone—as when Christ promises 'I will manifest myself to him' without mentioning the Father or Spirit—never excludes the others, since wherever one Person comes to dwell in a believer, all three are present together.
TRIN-B1C10: Augustine explains that when Christ 'delivers up the kingdom to God the Father' He will no longer intercede as Mediator between God and men, not because He stops reigning, but because the faithful will pass from living by faith to face-to-face contemplation, the joy Mary chose at the Lord's feet prefiguring that eternal rest.
TRIN-B1C11: Augustine formally states the rule he will use throughout: whatever Scripture says of the Son according to the 'form of God' asserts His equality with the Father, and whatever it says according to the 'form of a servant' he took by being made man asserts His subordination, so that both 'I and my Father are one' and 'my Father is greater than I' are simultaneously true.
TRIN-B1C12: Applying the rule further, Augustine argues that the Son's professed ignorance of 'that day and hour' means He withholds disclosure rather than lacks knowledge, and that texts giving the Father alone power to glorify or to have the Son 'not give' certain rewards are reconciled with the Son's equal, undivided share in the Father's power by the same form-of-God/form-of-servant distinction.
TRIN-B1C13: Augustine concludes that because one Person unites both natures in Christ, Scripture can rightly say both that the Son of man will judge and that he will not, and that the Father alone judges yet has given all judgment to the Son, since in the judgment only the visible form of the Son of man, not the invisible form of God, will be seen even by the wicked.
TRIN-B2C0: In this preface Augustine asks God's protection as he presses on to search the substance of God through Scripture and creation, declaring he would rather be corrected by any honest critic than praised by an erring flatterer.
TRIN-B2C1: Augustine adds a second rule to the form-of-God/form-of-servant distinction of Book I: some texts, like 'the Son can do nothing of himself but what he sees the Father do,' neither assert equality nor inequality but simply express that the Son is 'of' the Father, i.e. begotten, without implying any lesser working since the Father and Son act indivisibly.
TRIN-B2C2: Augustine notes that some texts, such as 'My doctrine is not mine, but his that sent me,' are ambiguous enough that they may safely be read under either rule, since 'doctrine' can be understood as the Son himself, so that 'given doctrine' simply means 'begotten as doctrine.'
TRIN-B2C3: Because the Holy Spirit never took a 'form of a servant,' texts about Him such as 'he shall not speak of himself, but whatsoever he shall hear' fall only under the second rule, meaning He is not less than the Father and Son but simply proceeds from the Father, receiving what is the Son's because all the Father's is the Son's also.
TRIN-B2C4: Augustine argues that Christ's plea 'Father, glorify me' does not prove the Father is greater, since the Holy Spirit also glorifies the Son and the Son also glorifies the Father, so mutual glorifying, on the same logic, would prove all three equal rather than one greater than another.
TRIN-B2C5: Augustine dismantles the claim that 'he who sends is greater than he who is sent': since the Son who 'came forth from the Father' was already present everywhere he was sent, being sent means appearing outwardly through the assumed creature (flesh for the Son, the dove and fire for the Spirit), not being sent by a superior, and the Father is never said to be 'sent' only because he never took on a temporal, visible form of his own.
TRIN-B2C6: Augustine distinguishes the Spirit's temporary manifestation as dove or fire, which did not unite that creature to his person forever, from the Son's assumption of flesh, which permanently joined humanity to the person of the Word, so that we say 'the Son is man' but never 'the Spirit is a dove.'
TRIN-B2C7: Augustine poses the puzzle that will occupy the rest of the book: if the Old Testament theophanies (the burning bush, the pillar of cloud, Sinai) were manifestations of God through creaturely forms, which divine Person, if any, was shown in each, and were the Son and Spirit ever 'sent' before the Incarnation and Pentecost.
TRIN-B2C8: Augustine rejects the crude view of some that the Son, as Word and Wisdom of God, is changeable and was directly visible in his own substance before the Incarnation, noting that even the human soul, though changeable, is invisible, so the unchangeable divine Wisdom is invisible all the more.
TRIN-B2C9: Augustine refutes those who read 'who only has immortality... whom no man has seen, nor can see' as applying to the Father alone and conclude the pre-incarnate Son was visible and even 'mortal' by nature; he proposes instead to inquire peacefully whether the Trinity indiscriminately, or one Person specially, appeared to the patriarchs.
TRIN-B2C10: Examining Genesis 3 (God walking in the garden) and Genesis 12 and 18 (God's word and appearance to Abraham), Augustine finds the text does not clearly specify whether Father, Son, or Spirit appeared, though the same voice that said 'Let there be light' seems to be the speaker to Adam.
TRIN-B2C11: Since three men of equal dignity appeared to Abraham at Mamre, rather than one figure standing out as greater, Augustine suggests this vision may signify the equality of the three divine Persons in one substance rather than the Son alone appearing with two attendant angels.
TRIN-B2C12: Turning to the two angels who came to Lot at Sodom and were addressed as 'lords' then as 'my lord' in the singular, Augustine considers whether this might represent two Persons of the Trinity, tentatively favoring the Son and the Spirit since Scripture nowhere says the Father was 'sent.'
TRIN-B2C13: Examining the burning bush, where 'the Angel of the Lord' who calls himself 'the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' appears to Moses, Augustine judges it uncertain whether this was a created angel bearing God's voice or one Person of the Trinity assuming a creature to appear and speak.
TRIN-B2C14: Reviewing the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt, Augustine again concludes that God plainly appeared through a subject creature but that Scripture gives no clear mark distinguishing which divine Person, if any one specially, was manifested.
TRIN-B2C15: Considering the theophany at Sinai (smoke, fire, trumpet, thunder), Augustine tentatively suggests the Holy Spirit may be signified, since the Law was written 'by the finger of God' (identified with the Spirit in the Gospel) and Pentecost's fire parallels Sinai's, though he stops short of asserting this with confidence.
TRIN-B2C16: Augustine addresses the tension between 'the Lord spoke to Moses face to face' and Moses's own request 'show me yourself plainly, that I may see you,' concluding that Moses's continued longing proves he had not literally seen God's substance, so the 'face to face' speech was itself only a corporeal or verbal sign, not a vision of the divine essence.
TRIN-B2C17: Interpreting God's promise to show Moses his 'back parts' but not his 'face,' Augustine reads the 'back parts' as Christ's flesh, seen and believed in through faith in the resurrection from within the Catholic Church (the 'place by the rock'), while the 'face' signifies the very form of God, reserved for the vision to come after this life.
TRIN-B2C18: Citing Daniel's vision of the 'Ancient of Days' bestowing an everlasting kingdom on 'one like the Son of man,' Augustine argues this refutes the claim that the Father never appeared visibly to the prophets, and closes the book concluding that no divine Person's essence is literally seen in these theophanies, only creaturely signs that Scripture sometimes, but not always, lets us attribute to a particular Person.
TRIN-B3C0: Augustine explains he would rather read others' answers than write his own, asks that readers be as free to correct him as he is willing to be corrected, and recaps Book II's conclusion that the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit (or the Trinity indiscriminately) appeared to the patriarchs through creaturely signs, setting up the unresolved question of how angels or creatures were the actual agents of those appearances.
TRIN-B3C1: Augustine states the remaining questions to investigate: whether the creature used in the theophanies was specially fashioned for the occasion, or whether already-existing angels spoke in God's person by assuming or transforming a body, and whether the Son and Spirit were truly 'sent' before the Incarnation and Pentecost in the same sense as afterward.
TRIN-B3C2: Before answering, Augustine lays down a governing principle: ordinary, continuously repeated natural changes (sunrise, tides, seasons) and rarer natural events (eclipses, earthquakes) alike proceed from the will of God as their highest cause, even though philosophers, seeing only proximate causes, fail to recognize this.
TRIN-B3C3: Using the extended example of a wise, holy man whose illness, fellow-laborers, and tools are all ultimately moved by God's will working through his obedient soul, Augustine argues that behind every visible, changeable effect lies the invisible, unchangeable will of God as the true first cause.
TRIN-B3C4: Augustine extends the example to the whole ordered hierarchy of creation—God governing angels, angels governing lower spirits and bodies—concluding that nothing happens visibly or sensibly except by the command or permission of God from His invisible, intelligible throne, so that the will of God is the first and highest cause of all corporeal appearances.
TRIN-B3C5: Augustine explains that what we call 'miracles' (Elijah's rain, water turned to wine, Aaron's blossoming rod, the serpent from Moses' staff) are simply God's ordinary governance of nature made suddenly visible and unusual, since He who ordinarily ripens grapes into wine or grows leaves on trees is the same God who does so instantly for a sign.
TRIN-B3C6: Augustine states the general rule that natural processes flowing in their ordinary, continuous, familiar course are called 'nature,' while the very same divine causation, breaking in unusually and abruptly for our instruction, is called a 'miracle'—diversity of manner, not of ultimate cause, is what makes something miraculous.
TRIN-B3C7: Addressing why Pharaoh's magicians could replicate some of Moses' signs (turning rods to serpents) but failed at the plague of lice, confessing 'this is the finger of God,' Augustine argues fallen angels can work only by a power permitted from above, given either to deceive the deceitful, warn the faithful, or test the righteous like Job.
TRIN-B3C8: Augustine denies that magicians or the demons behind them truly 'create' anything (frogs, serpents), arguing instead that hidden seeds for all future kinds of things were embedded in creation from the beginning, and that magicians, like farmers or breeders (including Jacob's colored rods), merely apply external conditions that draw out what God alone truly creates from within.
TRIN-B3C9: Augustine reiterates that God alone, as the one who assigns to all things their 'measure, number, and weight,' is the true Creator, so that both good and evil angels can only accelerate or combine causes already latent in the world, doing what they are permitted rather than creating, as the magicians' failure at the gnats (unlike frogs and serpents) shows they were purposely restrained.
TRIN-B3C10: Augustine classifies the ways a creature can serve as a sign of God—including a genuine created being changed for the purpose (like Moses' serpent), a thing newly made and then discarded (like the Eucharistic bread), or a human or angelic messenger speaking in God's own voice—arguing that consecrated bread is not thereby a literal appearance of God's own substance any more than the burning bush was.
TRIN-B3C11: Augustine concludes decisively, citing Hebrews' 'are they not all ministering spirits,' Stephen's speech in Acts, and Galatians' 'ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator,' that every Old Testament theophany—including those to Abraham, Moses, and at Sinai—was wrought not by God's own substance appearing but through the ministry of angels, who sometimes spoke or acted in God's own person, closing the book by promising to examine next how the Incarnation and Pentecost differ from these angelic theophanies.
TRIN-B4C0: Augustine opens by praising the humble self-knowledge of one who, awakened by the Holy Spirit, grieves his own sinfulness more than he prizes knowledge of the stars or the earth, and prays that only what God's truth breathes into him, not the figments of his own heart, will pass into his writing.
TRIN-B4C1: Augustine explains that we needed to be persuaded both how much God loved us (lest we despair) and what manner of sinners we are whom He loved (lest we grow proud), so that in the weakness of humility the virtue of charity might be perfected, and that the eternal Word, through whom all things were made, is itself the 'life' that is 'the light of men.'
TRIN-B4C2: Augustine explains that because sin left us unfit to partake of the Word's light, the Word was made flesh to cleanse us through the humbling of God Himself, since a sinner is not congruous to the righteous but man is congruous to man, and introduces the 'single to double' ratio: Christ's one death and resurrection answers to our two-fold death of soul and body.
TRIN-B4C3: Augustine details how our double death (of soul through sin, and of body through corruption) is met by Christ's single death and resurrection in the flesh alone, which serves as mystery for the inner man's renewal ('My God, my God, why have you forsaken me') and as a type for the outer man's future bodily resurrection ('handle me, and see').
TRIN-B4C4: Turning to number symbolism, Augustine explains why six is a 'perfect' number (equal to the sum of its own factors 1+2+3) and connects it to the six days of creation, the sixth age of the world in which Christ came, and the eighteen years (six cubed in months) of the woman bowed by infirmity whom Christ healed.
TRIN-B4C5: Augustine calculates that the forty-six years the Jews said the Temple was under construction, multiplied by six, yields 276 days—matching the traditional span from Christ's conception on March 25 to His birth on December 25—reading this as a numerical sign that Christ's body is the true Temple destroyed and raised in three days.
TRIN-B4C6: Counting the hours of Christ's death and burial to His resurrection, Augustine finds thirty-six hours (six squared) from evening burial to resurrection dawn, and forty hours (the biblical number of testing) from His death to the resurrection, seeing in the ratio of twelve to twenty-four (night to day-and-night) another instance of the single-to-double harmony.
TRIN-B4C7: Augustine explains that every prior theophany and prophetic sign existed to make 'the many' (fragmented, distracted humanity, scattered by sin into many desires) jointly proclaim the coming of the 'One' Mediator, so that through Him the many might be gathered back into unity and freed from the burden of multiplicity.
TRIN-B4C8: Citing Christ's high-priestly prayer 'that they all may be one, as You, Father, are in me, and I in You,' Augustine shows Christ wills believers to be united in Himself with the Father, so that the world may believe the Father sent Him.
TRIN-B4C9: Augustine clarifies that Christ did not say 'I and they are one thing' but that His own consubstantial oneness with the Father (in nature) is the model for believers' oneness in Him (through shared nature elevated to angelic dignity and through a will fused by charity into 'one spirit').
TRIN-B4C10: Augustine introduces his central antithesis for the rest of the book: as the devil, through pride, became mediator of death, leading man to fall through consenting to his own pride, so Christ, through humility, became Mediator of life, leading man back to life through obedience, since the devil (having no flesh to die in) could bring man only to spiritual death while masquerading as an angel of light through magic and false rites.
TRIN-B4C11: Augustine warns that demons can produce genuine but deceptive wonders through their aerial bodies, comparable to skilled but base human performers, and insists the faithful should neither despair at lacking such powers nor judge those who display them to be superior, since holy men and angels work far greater, undeceptive wonders through God.
TRIN-B4C12: Augustine argues that just as one man's sin brought death to all, the devil (mediator of death, who himself never dies in the flesh) drove humanity to fear bodily death more than sin itself, so Christ, the Mediator of life, teaches that death is not to be feared but ungodliness is, meeting us at death's door by a path opposite to how we arrived there—by righteousness rather than sin.
TRIN-B4C13: Augustine stresses that Christ's death was entirely voluntary ('I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again'), astonishing witnesses by how quickly He gave up His spirit, and argues that because the devil, being already spiritually dead, could gain no foothold within the sinless Christ, he was defeated precisely where he thought himself triumphant—by killing Christ's mortal flesh, the one avenue by which he could act at all.
TRIN-B4C14: Augustine argues that a true sacrifice requires a holy priest, an acceptable offering, and freedom from fault, and that only Christ perfectly satisfies all four elements of sacrifice (to whom offered, by whom, what, for whom) since He is simultaneously the sinless priest and the victim offered, uniting offerer and offering in one Person.
TRIN-B4C15: Augustine rebukes those proud philosophers who believe their own unaided reason can cleanse them to contemplate God directly, comparing them to travelers who glimpse their homeland from a distant shore but refuse to board 'the ship of wood' (the cross) that alone can actually carry them there.
TRIN-B4C16: Augustine argues that even philosophers who correctly grasp the eternal, unchangeable substance behind changeable things have no special competence regarding the succession of ages or future events, since their knowledge of the natural world's particulars (kinds of animals, seasons, and so on) comes from ordinary historical observation, not from eternal wisdom itself.
TRIN-B4C17: Augustine distinguishes several ways future things can be known—conjecture from past experience, aerial spirits perceiving events already underway from a distance, angelic revelation, or direct illumination of the mind by the Holy Spirit—concluding that pagan philosophers, lacking such revelation, cannot be trusted concerning the resurrection or the ages to come.
TRIN-B4C18: Augustine explains that because we were unfit to grasp eternal truth directly, we needed healing through something temporal congruous with our fallen, temporal condition, so the eternal Truth itself 'took a beginning' in time by the Incarnation, giving our faith (fixed on temporal events: His birth, death, resurrection, ascension) a path that will itself become sight when faith gives way to the truth it believed.
TRIN-B4C19: Augustine explains that the entire created order testifies to the Son as witnesses announcing His coming or confirming His arrival, and that the Son's being 'made' of a woman is precisely what it means for Him to be 'sent'—He is called less only insofar as He was made, without ceasing to be, before and beyond that making, equal to the Father by whom all things were made.
TRIN-B4C20: Augustine delivers his mature formulation: the Son is 'sent' not on account of any inequality but because He is from the Father as light's brightness is from light itself (of the same substance, therefore equal), and the Holy Spirit likewise is 'given' or 'sent' in that He proceeds from the Father and the Son, evidenced by Christ's breathing on the disciples before Pentecost, showing one Spirit given in two distinct, non-competing missions.
TRIN-B4C21: Augustine closes the book by comparing the Trinity's indivisible working to how memory, understanding, and will are each named separately by a single voice yet are always exercised together, concluding that whether the Old Testament theophanies or the sensible signs after the Incarnation (the Father's voice, the Spirit's dove) were produced through angels or some other creature, the Son and Spirit are never 'less' for being sent, only made known as from the Father, setting up the confrontation with the heretics' rational arguments that will occupy the rest of the work.
TRIN-B5C1: Augustine opens by praying for help in speaking of what exceeds human thought, and cautions that since God's nature is unchangeable and has no bodily qualities at all, we should not seek in Him any shape, color, size, or spatial extension, but conceive Him as good without quality and great without quantity.
TRIN-B5C2: Augustine explains that God alone is 'essence' or 'substance' in the fullest sense (from the Latin/Greek for 'being'), since He alone admits no accident or change, unlike created substances which can gain or lose attributes while remaining themselves.
TRIN-B5C3: Augustine states and begins refuting the Arians' key argument—that since 'unbegotten' and 'begotten' are said of the Father and Son 'according to substance,' and these terms differ, the Father and Son must have different substances—by showing that 'equal to God' is also said of the Son yet clearly does not imply different substance, so not everything said of God is said according to substance.
TRIN-B5C4: Augustine defines 'accident' as whatever can be lost or changed in the thing to which it belongs, whether by separation (like hair turning white) or by degree (like a soul being more or less wise), and concludes nothing accidental of any kind can belong to God, since He is wholly unchangeable.
TRIN-B5C5: Augustine introduces the crucial third category beyond substance and accident: relation, showing that 'Father' and 'Son' are eternally and unchangeably true of the divine persons yet are not said 'according to substance' (since neither is Father or Son in relation to Himself) nor 'according to accident' (since the relation never began or changes), refuting the Arian dichotomy that whatever isn't substance must be accident.
TRIN-B5C6: Augustine dismantles the Arian counter-argument that 'unbegotten' and 'begotten,' unlike 'Father' and 'Son,' are said 'in relation to oneself' and therefore according to substance, showing that 'begotten' necessarily implies 'of a begetter' just as much as 'son' implies 'of a father,' so both terms are equally relative, not substantial.
TRIN-B5C7: Augustine proves through examples from Aristotelian categories (substance, quantity, quality, relation, position, time, place, action, passion) that adding a negative particle never shifts a term from one category to another, so 'unbegotten' (not-begotten) remains just as relative a term as 'begotten,' referring to the absence of a begetter rather than describing substance.
TRIN-B5C8: Augustine states the rule that governs the rest of the book: whatever is said of God absolutely (in respect to Himself) is said of each Person individually and of the whole Trinity together, not tripled but in the singular—Father, Son, and Spirit are each God, great, good, omnipotent, yet together they are one God, one greatness, one goodness, one omnipotence, not three.
TRIN-B5C9: Augustine acknowledges the poverty of human language before this mystery: since Father, Son, and Spirit are genuinely three and not merely one Person under three names (against the Sabellians), yet defy being given a proper single-word answer to 'three what?', the Latin Church has settled on calling them three 'persons'—not because the word perfectly captures the reality, but so it need not be passed over in silence.
TRIN-B5C10: Augustine explains why the Trinity is called 'one greatness' rather than 'three greatnesses' by distinguishing things that are great by 'partaking' of a greatness distinct from themselves (like a great house) from God, who simply is His own greatness, goodness, eternity, and omnipotence, so that these attributes, said absolutely of God, are necessarily singular rather than plural.
TRIN-B5C11: Augustine notes that while the Trinity as a whole can rightly be called God, great, good, eternal, and omnipotent (all said absolutely), and can even be called 'the Holy Spirit' in the general sense that 'God is a spirit' and is holy, the Trinity as such cannot be called 'the Father' (except metaphorically toward creatures) or 'the Son,' since those are the proper relative names of individual Persons.
TRIN-B5C12: Augustine addresses the puzzle that some relative terms lack a reciprocal counterpart—we say 'the Holy Spirit of the Father' but never 'the Father of the Holy Spirit' (lest the Spirit seem to be His Son)—resolving it by noting that language sometimes simply lacks a corresponding word, as with 'earnest,' just as it does with 'the gift of the giver / the giver of the gift.'
TRIN-B5C13: Augustine examines the term 'Beginning' (principium), showing it too is relative (relative to the creature, as Creator is relative to creature), so that Father and Son together are not two beginnings of creation but one, and even the Holy Spirit, since He too works and creates, can rightly be called Beginning without multiplying the single Beginning that God is toward creatures.
TRIN-B5C14: Turning to the Trinity's internal relations, Augustine argues that since the Holy Spirit 'proceeds from the Father' (and, he adds, from the Son), the Father and Son together are properly the single 'Beginning' of the Spirit, and explains that the Spirit is not called a Son because He is 'given,' not 'born,' which is why He can also, uniquely among the Persons, be called 'ours' as well as God's.
TRIN-B5C15: Augustine raises a subtle question: does the Holy Spirit's identity as 'gift' depend on the moment He is actually given to someone, or was He eternally a 'gift' (something 'given-able') even before there was any creature to receive Him, concluding a gift can exist prior to being given, though a 'thing given' cannot be called such until it is actually given.
TRIN-B5C16: Augustine resolves how the Spirit (and God generally) can be spoken of in temporal, relational terms—'given,' 'our Lord,' 'our refuge,' 'our Father'—without any change occurring in God's own unchangeable substance, arguing by analogy with money (which becomes a 'price' or 'pledge' without changing in itself) that such relative predications register a real change only in the creature, never in God.
TRIN-B6C1: Augustine addresses the objection that Paul's calling Christ 'the power of God and the wisdom of God' implies the Father is not Himself wise but only the begetter of wisdom, refuting this by noting the same logic would force the absurd conclusion that the Father must also 'beget' His own greatness, goodness, and eternity as if these were separate co-eternal sons, when in fact power, wisdom, greatness, and the rest are all identical in God.
TRIN-B6C2: Augustine reasons that since the Father is only called 'great,' 'wise,' or 'good' together with the Son (whom He begot as His wisdom and greatness), and the Son is likewise only 'great' or 'wise' in relation to the Father, then whatever is said of God's substance is said of both together, not of either alone—except for the strictly relative terms (Word, Image, Son) that necessarily belong to the Son alone.
TRIN-B6C3: Building on 'that they may be one, as we are one,' Augustine argues that 'to be one' without further qualification (unlike 'one body' or 'one spirit,' which specify how differing natures become one) signifies identical essence, concluding the Father and Son are one according to unity of substance—which then forces the further inference that the Son must be equal to the Father in every single attribute, since inequality in even one respect would make Him wholly unequal.
TRIN-B6C4: Using the analogy that a person equal in courage must also be equal in prudence and the other virtues (since the virtues are inseparable), Augustine argues that in God, where 'to be' and 'to be wise, strong, or just' are simply identical, the Son's equality with the Father in one attribute of substance necessarily entails equality in all of them.
TRIN-B6C5: Augustine argues the Holy Spirit shares this same equality and unity of substance, proposing that He may be understood as the mutual love, holiness, or bond of communion between the Begetter and the Begotten—not by participation but by His own essence—so that the Trinity together is 'not more than three: One who loves Him who is from Himself, and One who loves Him from whom He is, and Love itself.'
TRIN-B6C6: Augustine explains why created things (bodies and souls) are inescapably 'manifold' rather than simple: bodies are composed of separable parts of varying size, color, and shape, while even the soul, though simpler than body, contains distinct and variable faculties (skill, memory, fear, joy) that can increase or diminish independently of one another.
TRIN-B6C7: In contrast to every creature, Augustine explains that God is 'manifold' only in the words used of Him (great, good, wise, blessed, true) while remaining absolutely simple in reality, since in God greatness, wisdom, goodness, and truth are all strictly identical with His very being; the Trinity, likewise, though three, is not to be conceived as 'triple,' since Father and Son together are no greater than either alone.
TRIN-B6C8: Augustine explains that while bodies increase when joined together (a married couple's combined body being greater than either spouse's alone), spiritual union works oppositely: a creature becomes greater/better by cleaving to God without God becoming greater, and since the divine Persons are already infinitely perfect, their union does not make God 'more,' which is why the Trinity is a Trinity, not something 'triple.'
TRIN-B6C9: Augustine wrestles with whether 'the one true God' of John 17:3 designates the Father alone (as the Arians claim) or the whole Trinity together, proposing that Christ's addition 'and Jesus Christ whom you have sent' implicitly includes the Son (and, through their inseparable harmony, the unmentioned Spirit) within the single title 'the one true God,' while deferring the harder question of how the whole Trinity, including the Son, can also be called 'the head of Christ.'
TRIN-B6C10: Closing the book, Augustine explores Hilary's formula 'eternity in the Father, form in the Image (Son), use in the Gift (Spirit)'—reading 'form' as the Son's perfect equality and beauty as God's Image, and 'use' as the Holy Spirit understood as the mutual love, delight, and 'sweetness' shared between Father and Son—and notes that all created things display a threefold structure of unity, form, and order that faintly traces, though never equals, this Trinity that made them.
TRIN-B7C1: Augustine resumes the puzzle of whether the Father is Himself wisdom or only 'the begetter of wisdom' by exploring, then rejecting, several increasingly absurd alternatives (that the Son is the Father's 'quality' rather than offspring, that the Father has no substance of His own apart from the Son), concluding that since divine simplicity means 'to be' and 'to be wise' are identical in God, the Father must be wisdom Himself, and the Son is 'wisdom of wisdom' exactly as He is 'light of light'—one essence, not two.
TRIN-B7C2: Augustine explains why Father and Son together are called 'one wisdom' and 'one essence' but never 'one Word' or 'one Son': 'wisdom' and 'essence' are absolute terms naming what God simply is, while 'Word' and 'Son' are strictly relative terms naming the Son's relation to the Father, so combining Father and Son never produces 'one Son' or 'one Word,' only ever 'one' of whatever is said absolutely.
TRIN-B7C3: Augustine explains why Scripture especially names the Son 'Wisdom,' even though Father and Spirit are wisdom too: because the Son as Word reveals the Father to us and gives us, His images, a visible pattern to imitate by 'emptying Himself' and taking the form of a servant, becoming an example for every kind of person (the healthy, the sick, the dying, the dead) to follow back to God; the chapter closes affirming that the Holy Spirit, too, since He is God and light, is also wisdom, so that Father, Son, and Spirit are 'not three wisdoms, but one wisdom.'
TRIN-B7C4: Augustine traces why the Greeks say 'one essence, three hypostases' and Latins 'one essence, three persons,' explaining that human language, lacking any word—specific or generic—that properly names what the three 'are' in common (since 'Father,' 'Son,' and 'gift' are not shared names the way 'man' is shared by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), settled provisionally on 'persons,' not because Scripture uses that word but because Scripture does not forbid it, unlike 'three Gods,' which the Shema explicitly rules out.
TRIN-B7C5: Augustine argues that strictly speaking, 'substance' (which implies something 'subsisting' as a subject with changeable qualities in it, like color in a body) applies to God only improperly, since God has no attributes distinct from His own being; 'essence,' by contrast (from 'to be,' as revealed in 'I am that I am'), applies to God properly and perfectly, since to be and to subsist are, for God, the very same simple thing.
TRIN-B7C6: Augustine closes the book by explaining, through the analogy of three golden statues sharing one gold (rather than genus/species logic), why we say 'three persons, one essence' without either persons or essence multiplying or diminishing when combined, then turns to Genesis' 'let us make man in our image, likeness' to explain that man is called 'after the image' of the Trinity (approaching it by imperfect likeness) rather than 'the Image' outright, a title reserved for the Son alone as the Father's perfect and equal Image.
TRIN-B8C0: Augustine recaps the equality established in Books V-VII and announces a new, deeper method for the books that follow, asking readers to keep firmly by faith whatever the intellect cannot yet grasp, as he prepares to move from argument about God to a more direct ascent toward Him.
TRIN-B8C1: Augustine argues that because in God 'to be true' and 'to be great' are identical, and the Father and Son together are not 'more truly' than either alone, two or three Persons together cannot be 'greater' than any one Person alone—unlike bodies or created minds, where truth and magnitude are separable.
TRIN-B8C2: Augustine urges the reader to strip away every corporeal and even every changeable spiritual image from their conception of God, insisting God is not any kind of magnified light, angel, or gathering of angels, but 'Truth' itself—glimpsed only in a fleeting, dazzling 'first twinkling' before the mind slides back into earthly images.
TRIN-B8C3: Augustine leads the reader through a meditation on the many particular goods (a fertile field, a healthy body, a virtuous friend) to the recognition of 'the good itself' by which all particular goods are judged good, identifying this with God, and explaining that a mind becomes 'good' only by the will's turning toward this unchangeable good, not by anything it can give itself.
TRIN-B8C4: Augustine argues we cannot love what we do not in some sense know, and since we cannot yet see God face to face, our present love of Him must rest on faith; he cautions that unlike our imaginative (and largely irrelevant) mental pictures of biblical figures we've never seen, faith concerning God's actual nature and deeds must not be allowed to 'feign to itself' anything false.
TRIN-B8C5: Augustine asks how we can love the Trinity by faith when we lack even the kind of 'general notion' (e.g., of what a human being is) that lets us picture and love unseen people like the Apostle Paul, since there is no other Trinity, and indeed no other God, with which to compare it by analogy.
TRIN-B8C6: Augustine reasons that we love a 'righteous man' like Paul not through any bodily image but by recognizing righteousness itself—a form we discern by looking within our own mind, since only a mind already possessing some standard of what 'righteous' means (found nowhere outside itself) could love or aspire to it, concluding that this inner form of righteousness, unlike the man who exemplifies it, is to be loved for its own sake, not by resemblance to something else already known.
TRIN-B8C7: Augustine identifies 'what is chiefly to be regarded' in this inquiry as true love itself, arguing that the two great commandments (love of God, love of neighbor) are so intertwined that Scripture often names only one and means both, and that God is to be sought not by imitating angelic marvels but inwardly, since Christ commended not His raising of the dead but His meekness and lowliness of heart as what we should learn from Him.
TRIN-B8C8: Augustine argues that anyone who genuinely loves his brother already loves love itself, which 1 John identifies with God, so that brotherly love and the love of God cannot in fact exist apart from one another—one who does not love the brother he can see cannot be loving the God he cannot see, since God simply is that love.
TRIN-B8C9: Augustine explains that our love for Paul's own recorded sufferings and virtues is kindled not from a bodily image of him but from a prior love of the unchangeable form of righteousness itself, by which we judge his life admirable—so that hearing of holy lives simultaneously strengthens our love of that unchangeable form and our hope that we, too, might live so.
TRIN-B8C10: Augustine reaches the pivotal discovery that will govern the rest of the work: analyzing love itself reveals three inseparable elements—'he that loves, and that which is loved, and love'—a trace of the Trinity found even in ordinary affection, and more purely when the mind loves nothing bodily but simply another mind, setting up the search, in the books to follow, for where exactly this trinity is to be found.
TRIN-B9C1: Augustine reminds readers that the inquiry is a genuine search, not a presumptuous claim to have grasped God, quoting Paul's 'not as though I had already attained' as the model posture, and states the method going forward: whatever is discovered about one Person must not contradict what is true of the others or of the Trinity as a whole, using as a test case whether the Holy Spirit is properly 'love,' since Scripture says 'God is love.'
TRIN-B9C2: Augustine applies the lover-beloved-love triad from Book VIII to the case of self-love, showing that when the mind loves itself, lover and beloved collapse into the same subject, leaving only two things, mind and love—not yet the sought triad—until we set aside the body and consider the mind as pure spirit, at which point he asks 'where, then, is the trinity?'
TRIN-B9C3: Augustine argues the mind cannot love itself without first knowing itself, and (unlike bodily sight, which cannot see itself without a mirror) that the mind knows itself directly through itself rather than by generalizing from having observed other minds, since it could not recognize another mind as a mind unless it already knew itself.
TRIN-B9C4: Augustine identifies a genuine trinity—the mind, its knowledge of itself, and its love of itself—arguing that when perfect these three are necessarily equal (since knowing or loving oneself either more or less than one truly is constitutes a fault), and that they exist substantially, not as accidents in a subject, since love and knowledge, unlike color in a body, are not confined to a single subject and can be directed elsewhere too.
TRIN-B9C5: Augustine shows that mind, knowledge, and love, while each a distinct substance in itself, are wholly and reciprocally 'in' one another (the mind is in its love and knowledge, love is in the mind and its knowledge, and so on), a trinity that is 'marvellously inseparable' precisely because losing any one member would destroy the others, unlike ordinary friends who can separate without either ceasing to exist.
TRIN-B9C6: Augustine distinguishes the private, ever-changing self-knowledge each person has of his own mind (which others can only take on faith) from the fixed, unchangeable truth by which the human mind as such is understood, gazed upon by many alike—an unchangeable inner standard by which we judge and correct even our imagined mental pictures of unseen things.
TRIN-B9C7: Augustine explains that whatever the mind beholds in eternal truth it 'begets' inwardly as a kind of word, which remains within even as it is 'spoken' through voice or gesture to awaken something similar in a hearer's mind, and that this inner word—whether about creature or Creator—is always conceived by love.
TRIN-B9C8: Augustine distinguishes desire (cupiditas), which loves the creature for its own sake and so corrupts the user, from love/charity (caritas), which refers the creature back to God and so rightly 'uses' what is inferior while 'enjoying' God and, in God, our equals—identifying love as the third element that binds mind and inner word together 'in an incorporeal embrace.'
TRIN-B9C9: Augustine distinguishes spiritual words, where conceiving and bringing forth are the same act (one who perfectly knows and loves righteousness is already righteous), from carnal or temporal desires, where conception (wanting) and birth (attaining) are distinct and never finally satisfying, since 'whoever drinks of this water shall thirst again.'
TRIN-B9C10: Augustine narrows his definition of 'word': not all knowledge is a word (we know things we hate without 'speaking' them approvingly), but knowledge becomes a true inner word only when joined with love or approval—even, subtly, when we rightly love our own condemnation of a vice we know and dislike.
TRIN-B9C11: Augustine argues that because knowledge is a likeness of the thing known, our knowledge of God, though real, remains unequal to Him (a lower nature knowing a higher one), whereas the mind's knowledge of itself, uniquely, is perfectly equal and 'on a par' with the mind itself, making that self-knowledge a true image and 'word,' equal to its begetter.
TRIN-B9C12: Facing the question of why the mind's self-knowledge is 'begotten' but its self-love is not (paralleling why only the Son, not the Spirit, is called 'begotten'), Augustine argues that knowledge is properly called an 'offspring' because it is something 'found' after a preceding desire or inquiry, whereas love is that very desire's fulfillment and continuation, embracing what is found—so mind, self-knowledge, and self-love form a genuine, equal, single-substance image of the Trinity, even though only the middle term is called 'begotten.'
TRIN-B10C1: Augustine examines the love of a 'studious' learner who desires knowledge he does not yet have, arguing that such a person never really loves the unknown thing itself but always something already known—the general excellence or usefulness of the kind of learning in question—using the example of wanting to learn an unfamiliar word like 'temetum' only because one already values understanding language as such.
TRIN-B10C2: Augustine surveys several ways people seem to 'love the unknown' (loving a person by reputation, loving a word one hears but doesn't understand, being simply curious) and shows in each case the love actually rests on some already-known genus, species, or the act of knowing itself—setting up the harder question of what happens when the mind seeks to know not something else, but itself.
TRIN-B10C3: Augustine argues through a chain of reasoning that the mind's very act of seeking itself proves it is not wholly unknown to itself: since it knows itself as seeking and as not (fully) knowing itself, it is thereby 'more known to itself than unknown,' just by virtue of recognizing its own search.
TRIN-B10C4: Augustine argues the mind cannot know or seek itself only 'in part,' since 'the mind' names a whole, not a fragment, and any partial self-knowledge would still be knowledge belonging to the whole mind—concluding paradoxically that since the mind wholly seeks itself, and nothing is truly absent from what it seeks, the mind is, in a sense, already wholly present to itself.
TRIN-B10C5: Augustine explains that 'know yourself' is not a command to discover a hidden fact but to attend to and live according to one's own true (rational, subordinate-to-God) nature, and that the mind's characteristic error is not ignorance of itself but forgetfulness—so absorbed in loving external, bodily things that it drags their images into itself and confuses them with itself.
TRIN-B10C6: Augustine explains that the mind errs specifically when it becomes so entangled with the images of bodily things it has loved that it comes to think itself is that very kind of thing (a body), retaining just enough rational judgment to distinguish external objects from their internal images—except in extreme states like sleep, madness, or trance, when even that judgment fails.
TRIN-B10C7: Surveying philosophers who thought the soul was blood, brain, heart, atoms, air, fire, or a mere blending of the body's elements, Augustine argues their error is not from ignorance of the mind (which they, like everyone, actually know intimately) but from an inability to conceive any real existence without corporeal images, adding a definition of 'finding' as the mind's 'coming into' what it seeks.
TRIN-B10C8: Augustine explains the paradox of the soul's self-inquiry: because the mind has, through love, become entangled with images of external, sensible things, it cannot conceive of itself apart from them, so being told to 'know itself' means not seeking something absent but withdrawing the foreign additions it has attached to itself, discovering it never actually stopped loving or knowing itself even while confusing itself with what it loved.
TRIN-B10C9: Augustine argues the command 'know yourself' is uniquely different from commands to know something absent (like the cherubim) or something requiring an external mirror (like one's own face): the mind knows itself by the very act of understanding what 'yourself' means when addressed, since nothing could be more immediately present to it than itself.
TRIN-B10C10: Augustine reaches the famous certainty at the heart of this book: however much one may doubt the nature or substance of one's mind, no one can doubt that they live, understand, and are, since even the act of doubting proves one lives, remembers why one doubts, understands that one doubts, and wills to be certain—an inner self-certainty untouched by uncertainty about whether the mind is fire, air, brain, or blood.
TRIN-B10C11: Focusing the inquiry on memory, understanding, and will specifically, Augustine argues these three, though each is fully 'life, mind, and essence' in itself, mutually and totally contain one another (I remember my whole memory, understanding, and will; I understand my whole memory, understanding, and will; and so with willing), demonstrating they are 'one life, one mind, one essence' yet genuinely three in their mutual relations.
TRIN-B10C12: Closing the book, Augustine identifies memory, understanding, and will (specifically the mind's ever-present memory, understanding, and love of itself) as the truest image of the Trinity found so far, while noting the difficulty that in this always-actual case the three seem to collapse together, and proposing that examining knowledge and love as they arise freshly in time—remembering what one did not remember before, seeing what one did not see before—will make the distinctness of the three easier to grasp.
TRIN-B11C1: Augustine turns from the 'inner man' to seek a fainter trace of the Trinity in the 'outer man' governed by bodily sense, explaining that although vision is the humblest of the five senses in principle, its excellence and closeness to the mind's own sight make it the best example to examine.
TRIN-B11C2: Augustine identifies a first bodily trinity in the act of seeing—the object seen, the vision produced in the eye (a real but transient impression, like a signet's mark in wax), and the will's attention that joins them—illustrating with afterimages and the doubled flame seen with both eyes that vision truly is a distinct, physically produced likeness, not merely raw sensation.
TRIN-B11C3: Augustine shows how this outward trinity of seeing is mirrored inwardly as a trinity of thought: the likeness retained in memory after the object is gone, the inner vision formed when the mind's eye turns back to that memory, and the will that unites them—together called 'conception,' now entirely within the soul rather than spanning body and mind.
TRIN-B11C4: Augustine describes how, when the will fully withdraws attention from present bodily senses to an inward image, the resulting mental vision can become so vivid that reason itself cannot tell whether a body is truly being seen or merely imagined, as happens in daydreams, sleep, madness, or prophetic trance, and notes that both desire and fear intensify this vividness.
TRIN-B11C5: Augustine concludes that this trinity of the 'outer man' is not the image of God, since it arises from the bodily sense of a lower, corporeal creature rather than directly from the mind, though even it bears some faint, common likeness to God as all created goods do; he begins mapping its three elements onto the divine Trinity, tentatively likening the visible object to a 'parent,' the vision to a 'quasi-offspring,' and the uniting will to something 'more spiritual' that suggests the Holy Spirit.
TRIN-B11C6: Augustine clarifies that vision counts as the will's 'end' or rest only with respect to a single, particular object of sight, since the will's true and only final rest is in beatitude; every particular act of will (seeing a scar, a window, then what lies beyond it) forms a linked chain of 'proximate ends' leading either toward or away from that ultimate blessed end.
TRIN-B11C7: Augustine turns to a still more inward trinity found in recollection alone (without present outward sensation): the bodily likeness already stored in memory (a 'quasi-parent'), the image copied from it into the mind's eye when we remember (a 'quasi-offspring'), and the will that unites them—noting this trinity is harder to analyze than the outward one because all three elements now share exactly the same spiritual nature.
TRIN-B11C8: Augustine explains that the will to remember something presupposes we already remember at least some fragment of it (we could not wish to recall 'what we ate yesterday' without already remembering that yesterday, and eating, exist), and shows that the will not only unites but also actively separates memory from present sensation—as when we read a page attentively yet retain nothing because our will's attention was elsewhere.
TRIN-B11C9: Augustine traces a chain of four successive 'species' or likenesses—the bodily object itself, the sense-impression it produces, the memory-trace formed from that impression, and the mind's inner vision formed from that memory-trace—with the will three times joining each 'parent' image to its 'offspring,' while noting he will not treat the intermediate step (sense-to-memory) as a distinct 'vision' in its own right.
TRIN-B11C10: Augustine explains that imagination can construct things never actually seen (a black swan, a four-footed bird) by recombining fragments genuinely drawn from memory, showing that even the wildest phantasy remains bound by 'the law of the memory,' since we can conceive no color, shape, sound, or size we have not in some way already experienced or assembled from experienced parts.
TRIN-B11C11: Closing the book, Augustine assigns 'measure' to memory (since only a fixed, remembered store of impressions is available to be recombined), 'number' to the multiplied visions that can be formed from that store, and 'weight' to the uniting will that inclines and settles the mind toward what it perceives or conceives—invoking the biblical 'measure, number, and weight' (Wisdom 11:20) as he announces the turn, in the book to follow, to seek this same trinity more truly within the inner man.
TRIN-B12C1: Augustine locates the boundary between outer and inner man: whatever the mind holds in common with beasts—sensing, remembering, and re-picturing bodily things—belongs to the outer man, and just as the body alone among animals stands upright toward heaven, the mind, its better part, should likewise be lifted toward the highest spiritual things, not by pride but by righteousness.
TRIN-B12C2: Augustine argues that although beasts too sense, remember, and combine images, only humans judge corporeal things by unchangeable, incorporeal, eternal 'reasons' (such as the rules of geometric measure) that stand above the human mind itself—an activity of 'higher reason' that beasts, lacking reason altogether, cannot perform.
TRIN-B12C3: Augustine explains that the same single rational mind has two functions: one that cleaves directly to unchangeable truth, and another 'diverted,' as a helper, to manage temporal and bodily affairs—comparing this to how Eve was formed from Adam as a helper without dividing his humanity, so that these two functions, though distinct in office, remain 'in one mind.'
TRIN-B12C4: Augustine insists the mind, though it has these two functions, is a single subject, and clarifies the key thesis of the book: a trinity can be found even in the whole mind considered as it acts on temporal things, but the true image of God is found only in that part which contemplates eternal things—the part directed toward temporal action, though also capable of forming a trinity, is not itself the image of God.
TRIN-B12C5: Augustine reports and rejects the view that the Trinity's image is found in a human marriage and its child—the man as Father, the child as Son, and the wife (who 'proceeds' from the man without being his daughter) as a figure of the Holy Spirit—noting that while this at least illustrates that not everything 'proceeding' from a person is thereby a 'son,' the rest of the analogy (making the Spirit a mother and spouse of the Son) is deeply improper.
TRIN-B12C6: Augustine refutes the marriage-trinity theory decisively from Scripture: since Genesis says God made man 'in our image, after our likeness' (plural) yet 'in the image of God' (singular), the text itself shows humanity was made after the image of the whole Trinity, one God—not, as the theory implies, requiring three separate human persons (father, mother, child) to complete that image.
TRIN-B12C7: Augustine reconciles Genesis ('God created man... male and female created He them') with Paul's statement that only the man, not the woman, is 'the image of God, but the woman is the glory of the man,' by arguing that man and woman together, as one united human nature, are equally the image of God, but that considered separately in her distinct role as helper concerned with temporal affairs, the woman figures the part of reason directed toward lower things, while insisting this applies to the sexless 'spirit of the mind,' where 'there is neither male nor female' before God.
TRIN-B12C8: Augustine describes the fall in psychological terms: when the 'inner man,' through the temporal-facing part of reason, 'slips too far' into outward things without restraint from the higher, contemplative 'head,' the vision of eternal things is withdrawn, leaving the soul naked of truth's light and reduced to covering its shame with fine words unmatched by good works.
TRIN-B12C9: Augustine traces sin's psychological root to the soul's prideful love of its own private power, which pulls it from concern for the common, universal good toward a mere 'part'—its own body—so that, entangled and 'polluted' by images of corporeal things fixed in memory, it either grows arrogant over less sense-bound souls or is swallowed in carnal pleasure.
TRIN-B12C10: Augustine distinguishes venial error in temporal action, undertaken with a good will toward truth (a common human weakness, easily pardoned), from active, willful 'fornication' of the soul, in which corporeal things are pursued as one's final good—warning, with the proverb 'he that despises small things shall fall little by little,' that this deeper corruption arrives only by degrees.
TRIN-B12C11: Augustine likens humanity's gradual moral collapse to a serpent's silent, scale-by-scale crawl: beginning from a perverse desire to be 'like God' (answerable to no one), the soul is instead thrust down to an intermediate grade of self-reliance and finally to the level of the beasts, its 'honor' (God's likeness) exchanged for 'dishonor' (bestial likeness), a fall from which only God's grace through Christ can rescue it.
TRIN-B12C12: Augustine reinterprets the Genesis fall as an allegory replayed within a single mind: the serpent as bodily sense offering illicit pleasure, the 'woman' as the mind's momentary, uncommitted consent to enjoy that pleasure in thought alone, and the 'man' as the higher reason's consent to actually carry the sin into deed—so that sin can occur in thought alone ('the woman eating without the man') or be completed in act ('the woman giving to the man').
TRIN-B12C13: Augustine notes, and declines to adopt, the view of earlier Catholic authorities that read 'man' as mind and 'woman' as the five bodily senses in this inner allegory, preferring instead to identify the serpent with bodily sense (since it, like the literal serpent, is 'more subtle,' being shared even with beasts) and reserving 'woman' for the mind's own lower, sense-engaging function, since Eve was uniquely formed for Adam, unlike any beast.
TRIN-B12C14: Augustine distinguishes wisdom from knowledge using Job's 'piety is wisdom, but to depart from evil is knowledge': wisdom is the intellectual contemplation of eternal, unchanging things (identified with the loving worship of God Himself), while knowledge is the rational governance of temporal action needed to avoid evil and rightly use changeable things—both good, but ordered to different objects.
TRIN-B12C15: Rejecting Plato's theory that all learning is really the soul's 'recollection' from a pre-existence (illustrated by a slave-boy's apparent geometric knowledge), Augustine argues instead that the mind is simply naturally fitted to perceive intelligible, eternal truths by an incorporeal light suited to it—just as the eye needs no prior memory to distinguish colors—and closes the book by announcing the search, in the book to follow, for a trinity within this temporal, rational 'knowledge' itself, parallel to the trinity already found in outward bodily vision.
TRIN-B13C1: Augustine turns to John's Gospel prologue to illustrate the wisdom/knowledge distinction concretely: verses about the eternal Word ('In the beginning was the Word... the life was the light of men') belong to wisdom's contemplation, while the temporal report of John the Baptist bearing witness belongs to knowledge, since we grasp 'there was a man sent from God' partly through ordinary human concepts and partly, regarding 'sent from God,' through faith.
TRIN-B13C2: Augustine explains that faith itself is a distinctly inward thing—unlike bodies, seen by all who look, or even other minds, only inferred—since each believer sees his own faith directly in himself but only believes it exists in others; it is called 'one faith' the way many individual human faces are called 'one countenance,' by likeness of kind rather than numerical identity.
TRIN-B13C3: Illustrating how some human desires are transparently common to all, Augustine tells the story of a comic actor who won thunderous applause simply by voicing aloud what every spectator already secretly willed ('you wish to buy cheap and sell dear'), and cites Ennius's observation that 'all mortals wish themselves to be praised,' distinguishing such shared but fallible desires from the one will every human being unmistakably shares: the will to be blessed and not wretched.
TRIN-B13C4: Augustine poses the central puzzle of the book: if literally everyone wills blessedness, and nothing unknown can be loved, why do people disagree so sharply about what blessedness actually is (bodily pleasure, goodness of mind, or both)—and, pressing further, can someone who refuses to live rightly (the only way to true blessedness) still be said to will blessedness at all?
TRIN-B13C5: Citing and endorsing Cicero's rebuttal of the popular saying 'all who live as they wish are blessed,' Augustine argues that willing something wrong is itself a form of misery, so that only the person who both has everything he wills and wills nothing wrongly is truly blessed—resolving the puzzle by showing all people really do know, if pressed, what blessedness in the abstract requires, even while wrongly seeking it in the wrong places.
TRIN-B13C6: Augustine asks why, given a forced choice, people generally choose 'having what they will' (even if their will is bad) over 'willing well' (even without getting it), arguing this preference is itself a mark of humanity's depravity, since a good will not yet fulfilled is actually a real good already possessed and brings one nearer to blessedness than a bad will fulfilled.
TRIN-B13C7: Augustine argues true blessedness requires being able to 'live as one wills' without limit, which even the most disciplined pagan philosophers, however admirably they bear hardship, cannot actually achieve in this mortal life (since they would still prefer, if possible, not to suffer at all)—concluding that faith in a life beyond death is necessary, since 'that cannot be which you will, will that which you can' is wise counsel for the miserable, not a description of true blessedness.
TRIN-B13C8: Augustine argues rigorously that blessedness is impossible without immortality: since no one is blessed while wanting something he lacks, and a blessed man cannot rightly will his own blessed life to end, a mortal 'blessedness' that must eventually be torn away against the will (or, worse, that one becomes indifferent to losing) cannot be true blessedness at all—hence 'life cannot be truly blessed unless it be eternal.'
TRIN-B13C9: Augustine acknowledges only faith, not unaided human reasoning, can assure us the whole person (soul and body together) will be immortally blessed, since even the best pagan philosophers achieved at most a hope for the soul's immortality alone (and inconsistently, at that); the credibility of this promise, he argues, is anchored in the Incarnation itself—if the Son of God could become mortal for us, it is far more believable that mortal humans could, by grace, become immortal children of God.
TRIN-B13C10: Augustine argues the Incarnation was not merely one possible remedy among others but the fittest possible one, since nothing could better prove God's love and rebuild hope than the Son's willingness to bear our undeserved evils first, so that the 'merits' by which believers reach immortal blessedness are themselves entirely God's own prior gift, given through the Holy Spirit poured out after Christ's resurrection and ascension.
TRIN-B13C11: Augustine raises the puzzle of how believers are 'justified in Christ's blood' and 'reconciled by his death' without implying the Father was somehow made more loving only after the Son died, resolving it by insisting the Father, Son, and Spirit worked this salvation together and in harmony, and that the Father in fact loved humanity even before creating the world—the language of reconciliation describing our change, not any change in God.
TRIN-B13C12: Augustine explains that humanity, through Adam's sin, was justly (though not directly caused) 'delivered into the power of the devil,' since God only permitted, and did not command, this abandonment—while still, even amid this permitted bondage, never entirely withdrawing His sustaining goodness even from the fallen or from the devil himself, who continues to exist only because God sustains him.
TRIN-B13C13: Augustine argues the devil had to be conquered by righteousness, not mere power, since the devil's own defining sin was loving power over righteousness, and it would not have taught humanity the right lesson if Christ had simply overpowered him; power, Augustine insists, is not evil in itself, but must always follow righteousness, never precede or replace it, in the properly ordered pursuit of true blessedness.
TRIN-B13C14: Augustine explains the 'ransom' logic of the atonement: the devil, finding no sin in Christ yet killing Him anyway, thereby forfeited his just claim over the sinners he held captive, since it is only just that those he wrongly holds should go free once he has unjustly slain One who owed him nothing—requiring Christ to be both truly human (able to be killed) and truly God (so that His voluntary submission to death, rather than mere weakness, is what commends righteousness to us).
TRIN-B13C15: Augustine describes the paradox at the heart of the Cross: the devil is conquered precisely at the moment he believes himself victorious, since in unjustly killing the sinless Christ he forfeits his just claim over sinners, whose 'chain' is thereby broken so that they may be 'turned from vessels of wrath into vessels of mercy,' as Christ told Paul on the road to Damascus.
TRIN-B13C16: Augustine explains why death and suffering remain even after sins are forgiven: these evils, though rooted in original sin, now serve believers as opportunities to contend for truth and prove their faith, and are permitted by God only so far as is 'expedient,' since none of the elect—those foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and to be glorified—will ultimately perish under the devil's power.
TRIN-B13C17: Augustine lists further benefits of the Incarnation beyond ransom from the devil: it shows humanity's true place in creation (higher than proud demonic spirits who lack flesh), commends grace as wholly unmerited (since Christ Himself earned His unity with God by no prior merit), heals human pride through divine humility, and models perfect obedience, whose reward is shown in the resurrection of Christ's flesh.
TRIN-B13C18: Augustine explains why the Son took flesh specifically from Adam's fallen race, and specifically from a virgin: taking flesh from the very race the devil had conquered fittingly ensures the devil is defeated by that same race, while the virgin birth—conceived by faith and the Spirit, without sinful concupiscence—ensured Christ inherited only the origin of humanity, not its inherited guilt, making Him alone able to serve as the sinless remedy for all others born through desire.
TRIN-B13C19: Augustine assigns everything the incarnate Word 'did and bore for us in time and place' to knowledge, and whatever can be truly said of the eternal, timeless Word itself to wisdom, finding both 'hid' in Christ per Colossians and further mapping John's 'full of grace and truth' onto knowledge (grace, tied to the temporal union of God and man) and wisdom (truth, tied to the eternal Word)—concluding that Christ alone, as the one Mediator lacking to the pagan philosophers, unites both, so that believers 'stretch through knowledge to wisdom' without ever leaving the one Christ.
TRIN-B13C20: Closing the book, Augustine reviews how the shared human will to blessedness, unattainable without faith and Christ's redemption, has been shown to require both practical, temporal 'knowledge' and (yet to come) contemplative 'wisdom'; he then locates a trinity even within believing faith itself—words held in memory, their meaning grasped in recollection, and the will uniting both, completed into a trinity 'of the inner man' only once these truths are actually loved, not merely held as possibly false—while cautioning this is still not yet the true image of God, whose fuller discussion he defers to the books ahead.
TRIN-B14C1: Augustine turns to human 'wisdom,' defined via Job as 'piety'—the worship of God—distinguishing it from the 'knowledge' of temporal, human affairs treated in Book XIII, and modestly declines to call himself 'wise,' preferring, like Pythagoras, only to be a 'lover of wisdom' (philosopher) who may still rightly discuss it.
TRIN-B14C2: Augustine argues that the trinity found in 'holding, contemplating, and loving' temporal faith cannot be the true image of God, since faith itself, being a temporal reality that will pass away once sight replaces it in the next life, cannot ground an image meant to be permanent and eternal.
TRIN-B14C3: Anticipating an objection that memory of faith would preserve this trinity even after faith itself ends, Augustine shows, through the analogy of a vanished bodily object still recalled by memory, that a trinity built on the mere memory-trace of a past faith is genuinely different from—not identical with—the trinity built on faith actually present, so neither trinity qualifies as the permanent divine image.
TRIN-B14C4: Augustine concludes the true, ever-abiding image of God must be sought in the rational soul's own permanent nature rather than in any passing state like faith, since the soul—however 'worn out,' obscured, or defaced by sin—never ceases to be capable of reason and understanding, quoting the Psalm 'man walks in an image' to show even a fallen, vain human being still bears that image.
TRIN-B14C5: Augustine considers whether an infant's mind, absorbed in and 'buried' by new sensory experience, can be said to 'know itself,' concluding that even an infant cannot be wholly ignorant of itself, though it is entirely unable to think of itself amid its overwhelming immersion in bodily sensation.
TRIN-B14C6: Augustine analyzes how the mind can 'place itself in its own sight' only by thinking of itself, without literally moving or dividing itself (unlike the bodily eye, which needs a mirror), concluding the mind's self-understanding is genuinely 'begotten' when it turns to itself in thought, though it was never truly unknown to itself beforehand, only unthought-of—establishing memory, understanding (intelligence), and will as the trinity's three terms.
TRIN-B14C7: Using the example of a musician thinking about geometry (who still 'knows,' 'understands,' and 'loves' music even while not consciously attending to it), Augustine clarifies that things stored in memory 'step forth' into conscious thought only when recollected, distinguishing knowing something from currently thinking of it, and recaps how Books XI-XIII progressively led readers from outward, bodily trinities toward this inward one.
TRIN-B14C8: Augustine states the chapter's central task: to find the true image of God in the mind's 'noblest part,' contrasting the mind's self-remembering, self-understanding, and self-loving (which involve nothing 'from without,' unlike the trinities of bodily vision or temporal knowledge) with those earlier trinities, whose objects were external or newly arising rather than eternally co-present with the mind itself.
TRIN-B14C9: Augustine raises, via Cicero's Hortensius, the question of whether the cardinal virtues (prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice) will persist in the blessed afterlife, where their present objects (danger, temptation, injustice) will no longer exist, tentatively suggesting all four might survive in transformed, higher senses (e.g., fortitude as unshakeable cleaving to God) even though their present, this-worldly exercise will have passed away like faith itself.
TRIN-B14C10: Augustine distinguishes the mind's self-knowledge, which (unlike knowledge of external or temporal things) never began at a point in time separate from the mind's own existence, concluding that because the mind has always remembered, understood, and loved itself since it began to exist, turning to itself in thought produces a genuine 'word'—the long-sought clearer image of the Trinity.
TRIN-B14C11: Addressing the objection that 'memory' properly concerns only the past, not the ever-present self, Augustine cites ordinary and even secular usage (Virgil's 'the Ithacan did not forget himself') to justify calling the mind's constant self-possession 'memory' too, extending the word beyond Cicero's stricter three-part division of memory (past), understanding (present), and forethought (future).
TRIN-B14C12: Augustine delivers the book's key thesis: the mind's trinity of remembering, understanding, and loving itself is the image of God not simply because the mind does this to itself, but specifically because the same mind is capable of remembering, understanding, and loving God—and only in actually doing so does it become truly wise, since human wisdom is nothing other than the worship of God, participated in from Him.
TRIN-B14C13: Illustrating with the everyday experience of being reminded of a forgotten acquaintance, Augustine explains that the 'nations that forget God' spoken of in the Psalms are not so utterly forgetful as to be beyond all possible reminder, but rather have 'turned into death' by their forgetting, and are 'turned to the Lord' again when admonition revives what was buried, not erased, within them.
TRIN-B14C14: Augustine argues that loving oneself rightly just is loving God (since the mind's true good is found only in God), so that anyone who fails to love God, though they still love themselves by nature, must in effect 'hate' themselves by pursuing what harms them—like the dog in the poet's image tearing at its own diseased limbs—and insists that even the weakest, most sin-darkened mind never loses its natural self-remembering, self-understanding, and self-love, which remain the very capacity by which it can still be turned back to God.
TRIN-B14C15: Augustine explains that the soul's longing for lost blessedness is not an actual memory of having once possessed it (which is wholly forgotten, known now only through Scripture's testimony about Paradise) but is rooted in its ever-present, ineffaceable memory of God Himself, and argues that even the ungodly, who do not live rightly, still recognize unchangeable standards of right living, 'impressed' on their hearts from the one Book of eternal Truth like a ring's seal in wax, proving they are not entirely cut off from that truth even in sin.
TRIN-B14C16: Augustine explains Paul's command to be 'renewed in the spirit of your mind... after the image of Him that created him' as referring to a single reality—one's own mind—being restored to conformity with the very God whose image it already is, clarifying that 'spirit of the mind' means simply 'the spirit that is mind,' not two separate things, so this renewal is not into some other image but the recovery of the mind's own original likeness.
TRIN-B14C17: Augustine distinguishes this renewal from baptism's instantaneous forgiveness of sins (comparable to removing a weapon from a wound) from the gradual, lifelong healing of the wound itself (advancing daily in the 'knowledge of God, in righteousness and true holiness'), a process of progressively transferring love from temporal to eternal things that will only be completed when the beatific vision itself is perfected 'face to face.'
TRIN-B14C18: Augustine considers whether John's 'we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is' refers to the future immortality of the resurrected body—since only the Son, not the Father or Spirit, took on flesh, our bodily immortality would properly conform us to His image alone, distinct from the fuller likeness to the whole Trinity discussed elsewhere.
TRIN-B14C19: Augustine concludes the book by favoring a reading of John's promise as referring chiefly to the mind's perfected likeness to the whole Trinity (since 'our image' in Genesis, not 'my' or 'your' image, points to the Trinity as a whole) at the final, unmediated vision of God, and closes by admiringly yet critically engaging Cicero's Hortensius on the immortality-seeking pursuit of philosophy, arguing that the pure love of truth, however admirable, cannot by itself suffice for wretched, mortal humanity without faith in the Mediator, Christ.
TRIN-B15C1: Augustine opens the final book by noting he has now traced God's image as far as the human mind, and states the task ahead: to show, so far as reason allows, that the nature above even this mind—uncreated, creating—is indeed the Trinity.
