TRIN-B15C2: Augustine reconciles 'seek His face evermore' with Isaiah's promise that God 'can be found when sought' by explaining that God, though genuinely found, remains incomprehensible, so the finding only deepens and sweetens the ongoing search—as Ecclesiasticus says, 'they who eat me shall still be hungry'—and defends his long ascent through creaturely trinities as no idle detour, since Wisdom itself teaches that God is rightly sought and seen 'by the things that are made.'
TRIN-B15C3: Augustine gives a compact, book-by-book recap of the entire work's argument to that point, from the Trinity's scriptural equality (Books I-IV) and the sending of Son and Spirit, through the substance/relation logic against the Arians (Books V-VII), the discovery of love's threefold structure (Book VIII), and successive refinements of the mind's image—mind/knowledge/love (Book IX), memory/understanding/will (Book X), the outer man's bodily trinity (Book XI), the wisdom/knowledge distinction (Book XII), faith (Book XIII), and true wisdom as remembering, understanding, and loving God (Book XIV).
TRIN-B15C4: Augustine argues that the created universe itself, quite apart from Scripture, teaches us to rank living above non-living, sensing above non-sensing, immortal above mortal, and so on, so that reason compels us to place the Creator above all these ranked goods as living, understanding, undying, unchangeable spirit.
TRIN-B15C5: Augustine reduces the many divine attributes (eternal, immortal, incorruptible, unchangeable, living, wise, powerful, beautiful, righteous, good, blessed, spirit) to the recognition that in God's absolute simplicity all are strictly the same single reality, then narrows them for manageability to three representative terms—eternal, wise, and blessed—since in men, unlike in God, wisdom and power, or blessedness and mere spirit, can come apart, making 'blessed' (which entails being righteous, good, and spirit) an especially apt choice.
TRIN-B15C6: Having reduced God's attributes to 'eternal, wise, blessed,' Augustine asks how this can be a Trinity, recalling that Book VIII's contemplation of unchangeable truth and love first let a trinity 'dawn'—one who loves, that which is loved, and love—and argues by analogy from the human mind (which cannot be wise without knowing and loving itself) that the divine Wisdom itself must, to be wisdom at all, know itself and love itself, yielding a trinity of Wisdom, Wisdom's knowledge of itself, and Wisdom's love of itself.
TRIN-B15C7: Augustine catalogs why the human trinity (mind, self-knowledge, self-love) fails to model God's Trinity precisely: these three are not themselves 'the man' but only belong to him, whereas the divine Trinity simply is God entirely; and in a human being memory, understanding, and love operate through each other sequentially, whereas positing anything similar in God (the Son understanding 'for' the Father) would collapse back into the very Arian error already refuted in Book VII, so each divine Person must be, in Himself, His own complete memory, understanding, and love.
TRIN-B15C8: Augustine explains Paul's 'we see now through a glass, in an enigma' by identifying the 'glass' as an image and clarifying that Paul's Greek word specifically means a mirror (not a watchtower), so that 'beholding the glory of the Lord' means seeing an image of God reflected in ourselves, being progressively 'transformed... from glory to glory'—from the glory of mere creation to the glory of justification, and ultimately of face-to-face sight.
TRIN-B15C9: Augustine defines 'enigma' technically as a species of the broader rhetorical category 'allegory' (itself meaning one thing understood through another)—specifically an obscure allegory, as distinct from a plain one like Paul's 'sleep' and 'darkness' imagery in Thessalonians—concluding Paul's 'through a glass in an enigma' together mean we see God now only through an obscure likeness, our own image, which even our clearest self-knowledge remains strangely hard to make out.
TRIN-B15C10: Augustine develops his mature theology of the 'inner word': every true statement is preceded by a silent 'word' spoken in the heart—belonging to no human language—which is 'seen' rather than merely 'heard,' as when Christ 'saw' the scribes' unspoken thoughts, since inward thinking collapses the ordinary distinction between speech and sight into a single mental act.
TRIN-B15C11: Augustine argues that the truest analogy for the divine Word is not our spoken or even silently-imagined sound-based word, but the pre-verbal 'word of the heart' begotten directly from knowledge—since, just as the eternal Word 'was made flesh' by assuming a body without being changed into it, our inner word similarly 'becomes' spoken sound without being converted into it, and a word is 'true' precisely when everything in it matches, without addition or omission, what is in the knowledge that begets it.
TRIN-B15C12: Augustine surveys and briskly refutes the skeptical 'Academic' philosophy that doubts all knowledge, showing that some knowledge—above all, 'I know that I am alive'—is immune to any deceptive appearance, including dreams or madness, since even a deceived or dreaming person is still, indisputably, alive, and that this self-certain knowledge can be endlessly (though never completely) multiplied by further reflexive acts of knowing that one knows.
TRIN-B15C13: Augustine draws the crucial disanalogy between human and divine knowledge: while God's knowledge is His very unchangeable essence, so that things exist because He knows them rather than being known because they exist, and His single eternal vision holds all times as equally present with no sequence of thought, human knowledge remains something distinct from mere existence, capable of being 'learned' and lost, making our derivative inner word radically unlike the Word eternally born from the Father's own simple, unchangeable essence.
TRIN-B15C14: Augustine explains that the divine Word possesses exactly and only what the Father possesses—no more, no less—so that the Father and Son 'know mutually,' each seeing all things simultaneously in a single, undivided glance rather than by shifting attention from one thing to another as human minds must.
TRIN-B15C15: Augustine catalogs further disanalogies of our 'word': ours can be false (when we are honestly deceived, not lying) and can concern mere doubt rather than settled truth, unlike God's Word which cannot lie; and since for us 'to be' is not the same as 'to know' (we can forget things and still exist), even our most permanent self-knowledge cannot yield a truly co-eternal inner word the way God's simple, unchangeable Word is eternally one with His unchanging being.
TRIN-B15C16: Augustine insists the Son of God must never be called God's 'Thought' (only His 'Word'), since 'thought' implies something formable that gains and could lose its form by being turned over in the mind, whereas the Word is pure, unchangeable form itself—and even in the promised future vision of God 'face to face,' when human thought will no longer flicker from one thing to another but behold all at once, the redeemed creature will still never be equal in nature to the uncreated Creator.
TRIN-B15C17: Turning to the Holy Spirit, Augustine notes Scripture carefully says 'God is love,' not 'the Holy Spirit is love'—leaving open whether Father, Son, Spirit, or the whole Trinity is meant—and argues from 1 John (love 'is of God,' 'God has given us of His Spirit,' 'he who abides in love abides in God') that the Spirit is specially, though not exclusively, called Love, since it is by receiving the Spirit that believers come to abide in God's love.
TRIN-B15C18: Augustine argues no gift of God surpasses love/charity, since without it even prophecy, miracle-working faith, and self-sacrifice profit nothing (per 1 Corinthians 13), while love alone, even without those spectacular gifts, brings a person to eternal life—showing why the Spirit, specially called 'the Gift of God,' is above all the gift of love itself, through which the whole Trinity comes to dwell in believers.
TRIN-B15C19: Marshaling texts on 'living water' and 'the gift of God' (John 4, John 7, Ephesians 4, Acts 2, Acts 8, Acts 10-11), Augustine shows Scripture consistently identifies 'the gift of the Holy Spirit' as simply the Holy Spirit Himself given—not a created benefit distinct from Him—concluding that since love is God's supreme gift and the Spirit is God's supreme Gift, it follows fittingly, though not exclusively, that the Spirit is specially named Love, since otherwise the 'Son of His love' in Colossians would absurdly make Christ the Son of the Holy Spirit too.
TRIN-B15C20: Augustine dismisses the Eunomian heresy that the Son is begotten by the Father's mere 'will' rather than by nature (which would make God's will something changeable and accidental, as ours is), preferring instead to say 'will of will' just as 'wisdom of wisdom,' and recounts a clever rebuttal exposing the self-defeating dilemma in Eunomius's own question about whether God begot the Son 'willingly or unwillingly.'
TRIN-B15C21: Augustine reviews how memory bears a distant likeness to the Father (holding all we know, even unthought), understanding to the Son (the inner word formed when known truth is 'said' in the heart), and will/love to the Holy Spirit (uniting the two, and requiring its own kind of knowledge to desire rightly), while insisting throughout that this is offered only as the best available creaturely analogy, radically unequal to what it images.
TRIN-B15C22: Augustine highlights a crucial structural disanalogy: in a human being, one single person 'has' memory, understanding, and will as faculties that belong to him but are not himself, whereas in God there are three full Persons, each of whom simply is the divine substance entire—not three faculties possessed by one divine 'person' but three Persons who together are the one God.
TRIN-B15C23: Augustine elaborates this key disanalogy at length: while the human mind's trinity of memory, understanding, and will constitutes only one human person, and these three faculties are unequal in different individuals and can vary in relative strength within one mind, the divine Trinity of three full Persons is nonetheless more perfectly indivisible and equal than any single human mind's inner trinity ever can be, since the divine nature admits no change or inequality at all.
TRIN-B15C24: Augustine warns that those who examine their own mind's structure with great subtlety yet refuse to believe it is truly an image of God gain nothing but self-condemnation from their own understanding, since their very failure to arrive at clear, certain conclusions about the mind is itself a mark of the 'penal darkness' and bodily burden that only faith in the Lamb who takes away sin can ultimately heal.
TRIN-B15C25: Augustine confesses that despite promising back in Book II to explain why the Holy Spirit, though proceeding from the Father, is not also called a 'Son,' he has found the distinction between generation and procession so difficult that no human illustration, including the analogy of a single human mind's will proceeding from thought, can adequately capture it—a mystery reserved for direct contemplation in the blessed life to come.
TRIN-B15C26: Augustine explains that because the Trinity is wholly outside time, there is no sequence in which the Son is begotten 'before' the Spirit proceeds, and argues that the Spirit, though truly proceeding from both Father and Son, is never called 'Son' precisely because no child (divine or human) simultaneously and identically proceeds from two 'begetting' sources at once the way an offspring would, so 'proceeding' names a different, non-generative relation.
TRIN-B15C27: Augustine reproduces a sermon he once preached to believers, explaining that Christ says the Spirit 'proceeds from the Father' (without denying He proceeds from the Son too) in the same spirit as His saying 'my doctrine is not mine, but the Father's'—referring what is properly His own back to its ultimate source—and closes by urging that where understanding fails, believers should simply trust Scripture's testimony and pray, live well, and seek understanding rather than deny what they cannot yet fully grasp.
TRIN-B15C28: The book, and the whole work, closes with an extended prayer of praise and confession: Augustine professes his Trinitarian faith on the authority of the baptismal formula and the Shema, admits that everything true in his fourteen books belongs to God while any error is his own to be forgiven, begs release from the burden of excessive words while defending necessary speech in service of truth, and prays that when believers finally reach God face to face, all their many, always-falling-short words will give way to speaking 'one thing without end' in eternal praise.
